newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks end down, but Hanwa impact slight.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks end down, but Hanwa impact slight.

text.p: Tokyo stocks ended a tad lower on the Thursday as earlier gains racked up by strong demand for blue-chip issues evaporated due to profit-taking, brokers said. The Ministry of Finance ordered Hanwa Bank to stop most operations but the news had little impact on trade.
The key Nikkei 225 finished at 21,143.34, down 46.62 points or 0.22 percent after clawing up as high as 21,301.26. Its December futures lost 50 points to end at 21,170.
"The overseas markets didn't panic on hearing the Hanwa failure news so that helped the Tokyo stock market keep its cool," Akihiro Naemura, strategist at Okasan Securities, said.

In pre-market hours, the Finance Ministry suspended most business activity of the bank sagging under the weight of 190 billion yen in problem loans -- the first time regulators have taken such forceful measures.
Trade in the regional bank's shares were suspended for the entire day on the Osaka bourse, but the benchmark Nikkei shrugged off the news.
"Worries about Japan's financial system have been well factored in the market, and the news was not surprising," said Yasuo Ueki, general manager of Nikko Securities.
Some brokers welcomed the government's move.

"Investors separate good apples from the bad," said Hiroshi Morimoto, Daiwa Securities' general manager. "The news did not discourage them too much because in a way the government is helping them by weeding out companies which are faltering."
After the market closed, the Osaka exchange said Hanwa would be delisted on February 22.
Avid interest in bellweather issues, which started on Wednesday, lifted the Nikkei average in the morning session as foreign investors and some domestic institutional investors continued to buy.
However, brokers said that gains were capped as selling pressure was intense at the 200-day moving average level at 21,235, and the Nikkei average was still stuck in a box range.
"The market is waiting for the Bank of Japan's survey on business sentiment due out next week for a push in either direction," Okasan's Naemura said.

Losers totalled 708 issues, advancers 371 and 173 issues were unchanged. Turnover was 362 million shares, little changed from the 360 million on Wednesday. In other indices, the TOPIX fell 2.17 points or 0.14 percent to 1,570.61. The Nikkei 300 lost 0.21 points or 0.07 percent to 295.55.
The second section index fell 10.26 points or 0.51 percent to 2,004.10. Turnover was 10.28 million shares against 9.67 million on the previous day.
Investors were busy buying shares of firms expected to do well, while getting rid of those which show signs of lagging.

Honda Motor Co Ltd hurtled past its lifetime high of 3,010 yen, rising 90 yen to close at 3,080, the most heavily traded issue on the first section of the Tokyo Stock Exchange in a turnover of 12.494 million shares.
Toyota Motor Corp, ranking second in turnover, set a high for the year, gaining 20 yen to 2,970 yen.
On the other hand, Kokusai Denshin Denwa Co Ltd slid to a new low for the year at 8,000 yen, down 260.

Large banks were unfazed by Hanwa Bank's trouble but some banks based in western Japan ended weaker. Fukutoku Bank, the largest percentage loser, shed 27 yen to land at 254 yen. Bank of Kinki fell 50 yen to 800 and Bank of Osaka lost 30 yen to 305.

Among sectors, automobile, air transport, precision instruments, railway/bus and warehouses were the top gainers. The leading retreaters were services, land transport, real estate, iron/steel and construction.
The over-the-counter index was down 12.37 points or 0.85 percent to 1,439.46 in late afternoon Tokyo.
--Masako Iijima, Tokyo Equities Desk (+81-3-3432-9052)
